title: No harm, no harm in return
hookLine: there is no harm and no returning harm
carry: start no harm, return no harm, remove harm
tomorrow: money goes missing. everyone's sure who did it. are they right?

lines: A HORN AT A GREEN LIGHT.
cards: A horn blares behind you at a green light. Someone cuts in line and doesn't look back. Your hand is already moving: the horn, the comment, the elbow.

Yesterday's question: if someone hurts you first, can you hurt them back? Hadith thirty-two answers in one breath, and it's worth hearing in Arabic, because it sounds like an echo: la darara wa la dirar.
No harm, and no returning harm.

teach.h: DON'T START IT, DON'T RETURN IT.
teach.b: Two nearly identical words. Darar is harm: don't start it. Dirar is harm that answers harm: don't return it.
Scholars read the pair a few ways, but the plain sense is a wall on both sides. Don't be the first to hurt, and don't be the echo. Now, careful: this isn't a rule that wrongs go unanswered.
The Qur'an allows a just response, measured to the wrong, and praises the one who pardons and puts things right.
What the hadith shuts is payback for its own sake, the extra twist that turns one harm into two. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR'S BEAM IN YOUR WALL.
teach.b: In Malik's Muwatta, this hadith sits among cases about neighbors and property, next to a report, also found in Sahih al-Bukhari, about a neighbor who wants to set a wooden beam in your wall.
Don't stop him, the Prophet said. Holy words, in the middle of plaster and beams.
Jurists turned it into a maxim: harm is to be removed. Not admired, not avenged. Removed.
So the question for any harm is practical: how do I take it out of the world, instead of adding a second one?

how: Muslim jurists use 'no harm and no returning harm' as a working rule of law, behind the maxim 'harm is to be removed', in cases about neighbors, property, contracts and family.

o: start no hurt, and don't hurt anyone back
a ban on going to court against a neighbor
a promise that nothing bad will happen to you

games.q: two words, one wall — tap the pairs.
p: harm for harm: don't return it
don't stop him setting it in your wall

s: if they hurt you first, hurting them back doesn't count
that's exactly the second word: la dirar, no returning harm.
the hadith means a wrong can never be answered at all
the Qur'an allows a just, measured response and praises pardon; the hadith shuts payback for its own sake.
in Malik's Muwatta, this hadith sits among cases about neighbors and property
holy words in the middle of plaster and beams.

games.q: your neighbor's tree drops leaves into your yard every day. you could hack it back hard, over the line, to make a point. what fits hadith thirty-two?
o: hack it back hard; they caused the harm first, so it's fair.
trim what's on your side and talk to them; no harm, no payback.
say nothing ever and take every loss; no harm means no complaint.
games.why: the hadith walls off both sides: don't start harm, don't return it. a fair fix that removes the harm is the point.

practice: Find something near you with a small mark on it: a chipped mug, a scratched phone, a dent in a table. Hold it and run a fingertip slowly along the mark; notice how small it is, and how it stays.
Keep it in your hand for the sit, and let one harm you've caused come to mind, one you could still take back out of the world.

wordCard.voice: No harm. La darar: start no harm. La dirar: return no harm. Two short words, one wall on both sides.

orig.note: Arabic: no harm, and no returning harm. the whole of hadith thirty-two's saying.

carryVoice: Your line: start no harm, return no harm, remove harm. Go gently.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah, hadith 32 (Abu Sa'id al-Khudri; Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni)
Malik, al-Muwatta', Book of Judgments (la darar wa la dirar; the neighbor's beam)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2463 (do not stop a neighbor from setting a beam in your wall)
Qur'an 42:40 (the recompense of an ill deed is its like; whoever pardons and amends, his reward is with Allah)
